input: In this worked example, the goal is to compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and to determine the fraction of reactant that remains after 60 min have elapsed. The measured rate constant for the reaction is k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, a value that was obtained by taking concentration measurements every 5 min over a period of 90 min and analysing how the concentration declined with time. For a first-order reaction, the half-life, denoted t1/2, is conveniently given by the simple relation t1/2 = ln(2) / k, which shows that the half-life depends only on the rate constant and not on how much reactant was present at the start. Substituting the measured rate constant into this relation gives a half-life of 15.1 min. In a similar fashion, the fraction of reactant remaining after a given time can be calculated from the exponential decay relation, and substituting the rate constant together with the elapsed time of 60 min gives a remaining fraction of 0.06. This result makes intuitive sense, because the elapsed time corresponds to almost four successive half-lives, and repeated halving over that span naturally leaves only a small fraction of the original material behind. It is important to note that these relations are valid for a first-order reaction only; a reaction following a different order would obey an entirely different decay law, and neither formula could be applied to it. In practice, the half-life is an especially convenient way of picturing the pace of such a reaction, because it allows the progress of the decay to be followed in equal steps of time, each step removing half of whatever remained at its beginning. The temperature at which the rate constant was measured should always be kept in mind, since rate constants are temperature-dependent and the quoted half-life and remaining fraction are strictly applicable only at the temperature of the measurement itself.
target: Calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction from the rate constant, and the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min. The rate constant is k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min. For a first-order reaction, the half-life, denoted t1/2, is determined by the rate constant alone, through t1/2 = ln(2) / k. Substitution of the rate constant gives a half-life of 15.1 min. The half-life does not depend on the starting concentration: each successive halving of the amount remaining takes the same time, and that constancy is the defining feature of first-order decay. The rate constant itself comes from the measurements: for a first-order reaction, the logarithm of the concentration falls on a straight line against time, and the slope of that line gives the constant. The fraction remaining after a time t is exp(-k t); substitution of the rate constant and of 60 min gives 0.06. The interval spans a little under four half-lives, and repeated halving over that span leaves a fraction close to the calculated value; the check by halving agrees with the exponential result. The fraction is dimensionless, a ratio of the amount remaining to the amount at the start. Both relations hold for a first-order reaction only. A reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither the half-life relation nor the exponential fraction applies to it. The rate constant is stated at the measurement temperature because the constant is a function of temperature, and the results carry that temperature with them. The measurement interval is short against the half-life, so the concentration record holds several points inside each halving, and the fitted constant rests on the shape of the whole record rather than on any pair of readings. The fraction remaining is the quantity a yield or a residence-time calculation consumes: it converts a time directly into the share of the charge that has not yet reacted.
